are not mandated by law, not practiced under business-as-usual conditions, and not financially 
viable without the project, and how they go beyond what would be achieved through existing legal 
frameworks. 
 
Additionality of Biodiversity Benefits 
Baseline Scenario 
In the absence of the Katingan Mentaya Project, the baseline scenario would likely involve 
continued forest conversion, peatland degradation, and biodiversity loss. This is due to systemic 
under-enforcement of environmental regulations, the economic attractiveness of plantation 
development, and weak land governance. Indonesia’s conservation laws (e.g., Law No. 5/1990 
and PP No. 57/2016 on peatland protection) exist, but enforcement is limited, particularly in 
remote forest areas. The project area contains globally significant biodiversity, including 
endangered species such as the Bornean Orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) and Proboscis Monkey 
(Nasalis larvatus), which would face escalating threats under business-as-usual conditions.

evidence.text:
Fire prevention: Remote sensing using fire hotspot data was 
conducted during the previous PD period in order to alert field 
staff to any fire incidences. On-the-ground fire suppression, 
management activities and patrols have also been implemented, 
and will continue during the next decade in order to reduce the 
threat of fire to biodiversity. As reported in the previous 
monitoring reports, the project has also established fire break 
plantations totaling 6.91 ha (as of 2020). During the next 
decade, additional fire break plantations will be established as 
per the project implementation plan (see the ‘Katingan-Mentaya-
Fire-Management-and-Mitigation-Report-Final.pdf’ report in the 
‘Anthropogenic threats: Fires’ supporting evidence folders for 
details). Furthermore, fire prevention and awareness training 
with project staff and communities will continue to reduce the 
impact of fires. These activities will continue to protect this 
important area of peatland habitat and the biodiversity it 
supports.

checks.question: Does the text show how baseline emissions are calculated, with an equation, parameter values or a numeric result?
Does the text address leakage (emissions shifted outside the project boundary), either by quantifying it or by justifying why it is zero?

evidence.text:
As there was no leakage during the previous baseline period, it is assumed that no leakage will 
occur. Actual leakage will be monitored throughout the project crediting period and will be 
reported at each monitoring event. If leakage occurs, the resulting emissions will be calculated 
following steps in the LK-ASP module.

• Before constructing any canal block that could impact areas outside the project area, 
surveys are conducted to determine whether the local population uses the canal (for example, for 
transportation, agriculture, fishing, or other activities). If no such uses are identified, a full block is 
designed and built. However, if any uses are found, the blocks are constructed with spillways to 
ensure that these activities are not affected. Spill gates regulate water flow and prevent any 
increase in water table depth outside the project area, therefore avoiding any increased CH4 
emissions or decreased vegetation production.

The integrity of the rewetting activities, along with the absence of ecological leakage, will be 
demonstrated during each monitoring event. Monitoring of ecological leakage will only take place 
on rewetted canals that have hydrological connectivity to water bodies outside the project area. 
It will be conducted through the installation of staff gauges and monitoring wells to assess 
hydrological impacts (flood and drought). The monitoring points will be established within 
transects with a radius of 1,200 meters from the canal blocking points. Each transect will be 
positioned perpendicular to the canal, covering both inside and outside of the project area. 
Monitoring outside the project area will be carried out wherever is possible, as there are 
community and land ownership constraints. Monitoring will be conducted regularly, with intervals 
ranging from hourly (using automatic data logger) to trimonthly (for manual data collection).

uncertainty threshold, no VCU deductions were made due to uncertainty. Detailed annual

Uncertainty BSL Workbook.

Figure 2. Industrial-plantation concessions on the similar-lands stratum, Indonesia: acacia (green) and oil palm (red). 
Industrial plantation is the dominant class acquiring similar lands; of these, only the acacia HTI licence is legally available 
on the project's Permanent Production Forest classification. Note: concessions intersected with the national forest map 
(2000) on peat; forest loss measured using Global Forest Watch (2011–2020). 
 
2.3 Data and methods 
 
The analysis followed these steps. (a) The national land-cover series (Indonesia Land Cover Map; primary 
and secondary dryland, mangrove and swamp forest) was used, and the 2000 forest classes were 
collapsed into a single continuous “forest at 2000” layer. (b) This forest-2000 layer was intersected with 
the national peatland map to obtain forest on peat. (c) The acacia and oil-palm concessions were 
intersected with this forest-on-peat layer to isolate the forest on peat inside those concessions e.g., the 
units within which forest loss over 2011–2020 was measured. (d) Because the national land-cover series 
does not extend to 2011–2020, forest loss inside those concessions was measured using Global Forest 
Watch (2011–2020) for the forest types of the national forest map. (e) Two suitability filters (slope and 
elevation, set to ±20% of the project’s range) were then applied to bring the retained forest closer to 
Katingan Mentaya Project’s forest-on-peat type, yielding 9,074,003 ha. (f) For robustness, an alternative 
suitability scenario was constructed from proximity to extraction infrastructure (within 30 km of a river 
and 40 km of a road, the greatest distances to the farthest point of the project); (g) this market-access 
scenario yielded a smaller, more conservative area of 8,932,940 ha (mask 2), which was adopted as the 
basis for the forest-loss analysis reported below. 
 
The two suitability proxies bracket the same result: the slope/elevation scenario gives 9,074,003 ha and 
the market-access scenario 8,932,940 ha, a difference of only 141,063 ha, with class shares essentially 
unchanged. The market-access scenario is the more conservative of the two and is adopted for the 
analysis. Under it the two industrial-plantation classes hold closely comparable shares of similar lands 
(acacia 13.2%, oil palm 13.6%) and importantly oil palm clears its holdings at a higher annual 
deforestation rate than acacia (5.46% yr⁻¹ versus 5.10% yr⁻¹), so identifying acacia as the agent of 
planned deforestation yields the lower baseline clearing rate and is the conservative choice. 
 
2.4 Application to Agents A, B and C 
 
Because the project area is 97% peat, near-flat and uniformly Permanent Production Forest, it forms a 
single dominant stratum, and the most-common-purchaser result applies uniformly across the areas 
assigned to Agents A, B and C. Agent A is documented (PT Kayu Alam Kencana, below); Agents B and C 
are the same class of agent on the same stratum. 
 
2.5 Conclusion

checks.question: Does the text describe a monitoring plan that names the parameters to be measured and how often or by what method?

evidence.text:
Each installed canal-blocking structure is equipped with monitoring wells (piezometers) located in 
the surrounding area to assess its effectiveness in raising and maintaining the water table. These 
monitoring points are used to evaluate the hydrological impacts of canal blocking on adjacent 
peatland areas. Water Table Depth (WTD) monitoring is conducted on a quarterly basis using a 
combination of automatic data loggers and manual measurements. The use of both methods 
enhances data reliability and enables cross-verification of recorded water level fluctuations over 
time.

The integrity of the rewetting activities, along with the absence of ecological leakage, will be 
demonstrated during each monitoring event. Monitoring of ecological leakage will only take place 
on rewetted canals that have hydrological connectivity to water bodies outside the project area. 
It will be conducted through the installation of staff gauges and monitoring wells to assess 
hydrological impacts (flood and drought). The monitoring points will be established within 
transects with a radius of 1,200 meters from the canal blocking points. Each transect will be 
positioned perpendicular to the canal, covering both inside and outside of the project area. 
Monitoring outside the project area will be carried out wherever is possible, as there are 
community and land ownership constraints. Monitoring will be conducted regularly, with intervals 
ranging from hourly (using automatic data logger) to trimonthly (for manual data collection).

The Katingan Mentaya Project employs a comprehensive biodiversity and forest monitoring 
framework to assess and enhance conservation outcomes. Indicators for carbon monitoring, 
including field plot data and remotely sensed imagery, track natural forest regeneration, which 
serves as a proxy for forest quality and its suitability to support RTE species. Additionally, line 
transect surveys, camera trapping, and opportunistic observations are used to document RTE 
species. While these methods are not designed to provide precise population density estimates, 
they are both cost-effective and feasible, offering valuable insights into species presence and 
relative abundance indices. 
 
Key species monitoring includes ground nest surveys for Bornean Orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus), 
the project’s key trigger species, to track population trends over time. Plans for future monitoring 
periods include freshwater fish surveys to document species within aquatic habitats. Regular 
patrols will also document signs of anthropogenic disturbance, such as logging camps, timber piles, 
and used shotgun cartridges. The Community Engagement team plays a critical role in addressing 
and monitoring ongoing hunting activities to mitigate pressures on wildlife populations. 
 
Biodiversity monitoring spans the entire project area, with a particular focus on different habitat 
types and key species. A suite of tailored field survey methods is applied to different taxa and are 
detailed in Table 5.5. Community interviews further enrich the monitoring process by assessing 
local harvest practices and threats to biodiversity. To evaluate conservation success, rigorous data

The Katingan Project has not been registered under any emissions trading programs but may 
seek to do so in the future. In this case applicable requirements in the VCS Standard, AFOLU 
Requirements, and the Registration and Issuance process will be followed. The project will not 
claim credit for the same GHG emission reduction or removal under the VCS Program and 
another GHG program.

The verification team is not aware of project involvement in other forms of environmental credits 
from its activities. The project has not been registered, and is not seeking registration, under any 
other GHG programs. The Katingan Project currently only seeks carbon credits under the VCS 
program. This was confirmed through a risk-based internet review and interview with Project 
Proponents. Therefore, the verification team deems the project eligible to participate under the 
VCS Program.

There were no methodology deviations or PD deviations during this relating to monitoring period 
(please see Section 3.2). The GHG emission reductions generated by the project are not included 
in an emissions trading program other than the VCS program.  The Project Proponent has not 
received or sought any other form of environmental credit as confirmed through a risk-based 
review by the verification team (see Section 3.1).

The audit team performed a web based review of current GHG programs and found no 
evidence of the project being registered under any other program

evidence.text:
Emission Trading Programs and Other Binding Limits: During this monitoring period, activities 
carried out by the project are not covered by any emission trading programs or other binding 
limits in relation to GHG emissions. Presidential Decree No. 61/2011 regarding the National 
Action Plan for Reducing Green House Gas Emissions requires government agencies to set 
reduction targets for specific sectors and identify plans for achieving these goals. The project 
is not currently subject to these targets nor will its reductions be used to demonstrate 
achievement of the agency goals.

Other Forms of Environmental Credit: The Katingan Project currently only seeks carbon 
credits under the VCS program, and has not received other forms of environmental credits 
from its activities.
2.6.2 Double Claiming, Other Forms of Credit, and Scope 3 Emissions (VCS, 3.24)

No Double Claiming with Emissions Trading Programs or Binding Emission Limits

program or binding emission limit? See the VCS Program Definitions for definitions of 
emissions trading program and binding emission limit.

checks.question: Does the text address the host country's national accounting or registry, or a corresponding adjustment?

evidence.text:
Financial Services Authority (OJK) Regulation No. 14/2023 on Carbon Trading in the Carbon 
Exchange. The project is registered under the SRN PPI with registration number REG-11-PR-X-
2025-6737. Although the SRUK registry is not yet available at the time of the preparation of the 
PD, the recently launched registry system of Indonesia ensures transparency and prevents 
double counting, meaning that even if voluntary credits are sold to foreigners, the emissions 
reductions remain as Indonesian assets toward their NDC. 
 
 
2. Regional and Local Environmental Regulations 
 
Peatland and Forest Fire Management 
Presidential Instruction (INPRES) No. 10/2011 and subsequent renewals regarding Peatland 
Management 
Government Regulation PP No. 71/2014 on Protection and Management of Peatland Ecosystems 
Regional Regulation of Central Kalimantan Province No. 1/2020 on Forest Fire Control 
 
Sustainable Land and Water Management 
Ministry of Environment and Forestry Decree No. P.15/MENLHK/SETJEN/KUM.1/2/2017 on 
Water Table Measurement in Peat Ecosystems 
Ministry of Environment and Forestry Regulation No. 60/MENLHK/Setjen/Kum.1/10/2019 on 
Peat Ecosystem Management 
 
3. Compliance Assurance Measures 
The Katingan Mentaya Project adheres to these regulations through the following mechanisms:

Indonesia National Registry System: With the issuance of Ministry of Environment and Forestry 
no P70, P71, P72 and P73 in late December 2017, REDD projects within the jurisdiction of 
Indonesia should now be registered with the newly created National Registry System. It is also 
proposed that this may in turn make projects eligible to receive Result Based Payments for 
avoided emissions. However, up to date, this law is not enforced and supporting regulation and 
institution are still being developed and yet to be trialed. Therefore, avoided carbon emissions 
generated in this monitoring period are unaffected by this regulation.

checks.question: Does the text describe a stakeholder consultation with specifics such as dates, places, participants or comments received?

evidence.text:
All project activities were designed and implemented in participation with project-zone 
communities and based on full consultation and FPIC principles. The project has continuously 
promoted collaborative management, as described in Section 3.1.7. An example of this is the 
development of collaboration management areas within the project area, including one that 
involves community members living near the Hantipan Canal and in the North Eastern area. A 
partnership scheme has been agreed between Kampung Melayu village, Telaga village and the 
project to ensure tenurial rights are fully recognized. Through the partnership, a community-led 
agroforestry initiative has been developed, which has been designed to generate local income 
and has included the planting of various native tree species. The partnership was established 
following a formal process, involving central and local government institutions, community 
organizers, representatives from the villages, and the project staff. Spatial planning, area 
delineation, and the agroforestry technical concept were made in collaboration with the two 
villages. For further details about activities related to this community-led agroforestry initiative 
during this monitoring period, please see Section 5.2.3.3.

checks.question: Does the text describe a grievance or complaint mechanism through which affected people can raise concerns?

evidence.text:
Information Materials: The project distributes brochures, flyers, and posters throughout the 
community centres and public gathering spots, detailing the steps to file a grievance, contact 
information for zona managers, and the types of issues that can be addressed through this 
mechanism. 
 
Accessibility of the Grievance Mechanism 
Multiple Reporting Channels: Grievances can be reported not just in person but also via 
dedicated phone lines, email addresses, and a project-specific app, if available. This multi-
channel approach ensures that villagers can submit their grievances in a manner that is most 
convenient and accessible to them. 
 
Assistance in Grievance Filing: For individuals who may need assistance in articulating their 
grievances, such as the elderly or those who are illiterate, project staff provide support in 
documenting and filing their complaints to ensure everyone could be heard. 
 
Documentation and Public Availability 
SIRETA Database: All grievances, whether they are validated or not, are recorded in the SIRETA 
database. This centralised system includes detailed entries of each case, such as the nature of 
the grievance, the stakeholders involved, the responses provided, and the resolution status. 
 
Transparency in Documentation: Once a grievance is resolved, all relevant documentation 
including minutes of meetings, agreements, and photographic evidence, is uploaded to the 
database. This not only maintains a record of the issue and its resolution but also ensures that 
the process is transparent. 
 
Public Access to Information: Key summaries of grievance cases and their resolutions are 
periodically shared with the community through public meetings and posted on the project’s 
official website. For sensitive issues, privacy is maintained by anonymising the details that could 
identify the individuals involved. 
 
Feedback Loops: The project incorporates feedback received about the grievance process itself 
into ongoing improvements, ensuring the mechanism remains effective and responsive to 
community needs.

checks.question: Does the text report an environmental impact assessment or an analysis of the project's environmental risks?

evidence.text:
In our commitment to sustainable community engagement and the application of the 
precautionary principle, we have established measures to mitigate potential negative impacts on 
community well-being, particularly for vulnerable groups such as women, girls, children, and other 
marginalised populations, as well as for the maintenance and enhancement of high conservation 
value (HCV) attributes related to community well-being.  
 
Current and Future Measures for Community Well-being and Environmental Protection  
 
Participatory Planning and Consultation 
We have implemented a participatory planning process, central to which are ongoing 
consultations with community members. This approach facilitates the early identification and 
discussion of potential negative impacts, such as air and noise pollution, water discharges, waste 
generation, and the release of hazardous materials. By directly involving community members, 
especially representatives of vulnerable groups, we ensure that our project design addresses 
their unique needs and concerns (UNDP, 2018; IFC Performance Standard 1). This collaborative 
approach promotes shared ownership of both the project and the outcomes, fostering trust and 
transparency (WHO, 2020). 
 
Proactive Risk Assessment and Precautionary Planning 
In alignment with the precautionary principle (Rio Declaration, 1992), we conduct risk 
assessments that consider both scientifically substantiated risks and potential risks for which 
conclusive evidence may be lacking. This forward-looking strategy prioritises preventive action, 
ensuring that we address potential threats to community well-being before they materialise 
(IPBES, 2019). This includes designing strategies to minimise emissions, control waste, and limit 
noise, as well as implementing spill prevention protocols to protect water quality and prevent 
contamination (IFC Performance Standard 4). 
 
Monitoring and Responsive Adaptation 
Based on our ongoing monitoring and insights gathered through team interactions with the 
community, no significant adverse effects have been recorded to date. However, we remain 
vigilant. Monitoring systems are in place to identify early signs of potential impacts on community 
well-being or HCV attributes, allowing us to adapt our strategies as needed (HCV Resource 
Network). By prioritising community feedback, we ensure that adjustments are responsive to 
emerging issues or unforeseen challenges (IFC Performance Standard 1). 
 
Safety and Inclusivity Measures for Vulnerable Groups 
Specific measures to safeguard women, girls, children, and other marginalised groups are 
embedded in our project design (UNDP, 2018). For example, we implement safe worksite 
protocols (ILO, 1992), maintain accessible communication channels for reporting concerns, and 
promote training programmes on environmental safety and personal security (WHO, 2020). These 
proactive actions provide a secure environment and support community empowerment by 
equipping individuals with knowledge and resources to contribute to and benefit from the project 
sustainably. 
 
Alignment with the Precautionary Principle 
These measures exemplify our commitment to the precautionary principle, where we prioritise the 
prevention of harm even in the absence of complete scientific certainty (Rio Declaration, 1992). 
Our approach reflects the belief that safeguarding community well-being and protecting 
environmental attributes are foundational to achieving sustainable, long-term outcomes (IPBES, 
2019). This forward-thinking stance ensures that the health, safety, and rights of all community 
members remain central to our operational philosophy.

checks.question: Does the text address the rights of local communities or indigenous peoples, such as free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) or benefit sharing?

evidence.text:
The Katingan Project adopts FPIC principles in all community consultation processes (see 
Figure 2). This approach has been and will be maintained throughout the life of the project. It 
allows local people to critically consider potential impacts of the project and to negotiate based 
on mutual consensus without being forced or manipulated. The FPIC approach is also used 
for stakeholder consultations and communications which were discussed earlier in this report.
